script: [serious] On the morning of June 12th, 1962, the guards at Alcatraz walked the cellblock for the morning count. In cell after cell, men were getting up. But in three cells, the prisoners didn't move. A guard reached through the bars and touched one of them. The head rolled off the pillow and onto the floor. It wasn't a head. It was a dummy, made of soap, toilet paper and paint, with real human hair swept up from the prison barbershop floor. The men it was meant to hide, Frank Morris and the brothers John and Clarence Anglin, were gone. Alcatraz was supposed to be escape-proof. A rock in the middle of San Francisco Bay, surrounded by cold water and strong currents. In its twenty-nine years as a federal prison, thirty-six men tried to escape it. Almost all of them were caught, shot, or drowned. This is the complete case file on the one escape that may have worked. Let's open it. Alcatraz opened as a federal prison in 1934. It was built for the men other prisons couldn't hold. Al Capone served time there. So did Machine Gun Kelly. Every prisoner had his own cell. The count happened again and again, every day. And the island itself was the final wall. Even a man who got out of the building still had more than a mile of freezing water between him and the city. Frank Morris arrived in January 1960. He was a career criminal, a bank robber and burglar with a long record of breaking out of other prisons, and people who knew him called him quiet and very intelligent. The Anglin brothers, bank robbers from Florida, arrived soon after. All three knew each other from earlier prisons. So did a fourth man, Allen West, who was already on the island. And somehow, the four of them ended up in cells side by side. Starting in December 1961, the four men began building an escape in plain sight. Behind each cell, under the sink, was a small air vent leading into an unguarded utility corridor. Using metal spoons taken from the dining hall, discarded saw blades, and a drill they improvised from the motor of a broken vacuum cleaner, they slowly widened the vents, chip by chip, and hid the holes behind cardboard painted to look like the wall. To cover the noise, Morris played an accordion during music hour. Night after night, they dug. Once through, they climbed the pipes inside the corridor to the top of the cellblock, and there, out of sight of the guards, they built a secret workshop. They made the heads. They made wooden paddles. They made life vests. And, from more than fifty stolen raincoats, sealed with the heat of the prison's own steam pipes, they made a raft. They even took a concertina, a small squeezebox instrument, to use as a pump to blow it up. At the very top, they pried open a ventilator to the roof, and held it in place with a fake bolt made of soap. On the night of June 11th, the dummies went into the beds, tucked under blankets with towels and clothes to look like sleeping men. Morris and the Anglins crawled out through their vents. Allen West could not. The cement he had used to patch his vent had hardened, and by the time he broke through, the others were gone. He would later tell investigators everything. The three men climbed up through the corridor, out through the ventilator onto the roof, and slid down a pipe to the ground. They crossed to the northeast shore of the island, out of reach of the searchlights. There, they inflated the raft, and pushed off into the dark water of the bay. According to West, the plan was to reach Angel Island, cross to the mainland, steal clothes and a car, and disappear. That is the last time anyone can say for certain where they were. By morning, the island was on lockdown, and the FBI was running one of the biggest manhunts of its time. The FBI's own memo, written that evening at 7:28 p.m., reports that investigation has failed to locate the subjects at the prison or on the island, and no trace of them has been found on the mainland or in the water. Over the following days, the search turned up pieces. A paddle of the type the men used, floating in the bay between Alcatraz and Angel Island. Then, a waterproof packet wrapped in rubber, holding personal letters belonging to the Anglins. Scraps of rubber washed up near the Golden Gate Bridge. And a homemade life vest came ashore near Fort Cronkhite. But no bodies were ever found. And that packet raises the question that has haunted the case ever since. If you expected to drown, why would you seal your letters in waterproof rubber? In 1979, the FBI closed its investigation. It concluded the men were unlikely to have survived the cold water and currents. The case was handed to the U.S. Marshals Service. And the Marshals never closed it. Less than a year after the escape, in 1963, Alcatraz itself was shut down. The case against survival is simple. The water in the bay is cold enough to kill. The currents are strong. Three men, on a homemade raft, at night, and no theft of clothes or a car was ever tied to them. The FBI believed they drowned, or died of cold, somewhere in the bay. But there is another side. Just six months later, in December 1962, another prisoner, John Paul Scott, escaped Alcatraz and made it through the water all the way to a San Francisco beach. He was found there and taken back. But he proved one thing. The bay could be crossed. And a raft is better than swimming. In 1975, a family friend named Fred Brizzi said he had met the brothers in Brazil. He gave the family a photograph of two men on a farm, one of them bearded, both in sunglasses, and said it was John and Clarence. It was never confirmed. Then, in 2013, the San Francisco police received a letter. It said: My name is John Anglin. I escaped from Alcatraz in June 1962 with my brother Clarence and Frank Morris. I'm 83 years old and in bad shape. I have cancer. It said all three of them made it that night, but barely. The FBI tested the letter for fingerprints, DNA and handwriting. The results were inconclusive, and its author has never been found. Here is what the file really tells us. These men planned for months, and they planned to live. They took life vests and paddles, and their letters, sealed against the water. Whether the bay took them that night, or whether three men got away with the most famous escape in American history, nobody has ever proven. In 2022, sixty years after the escape, the U.S. Marshals released new age-progressed images of all three men, showing how they might look in their nineties. The Marshals say they will keep the case open, and keep following tips, until the men would be around a hundred years old. Because officially, Frank Morris, John Anglin and Clarence Anglin are not dead. They are fugitives. So, did they make it? Tell me in the comments. This is Dossier Decoded. Case file: The Alcatraz Escape. Closed by the FBI. Still open.
